explain.say: On 7 June 2020 protesters in Bristol pulled down a bronze statue of Edward Colston and rolled it into the harbour. Colston was a seventeenth-century merchant in the Royal African Company, which shipped many thousands of enslaved Africans. Public history is the history people meet outside books: statues, museums, films. Look at this statue's life on the timeline.

explain.say: See the first dot. The statue went up in 1895, almost two centuries after Colston died, to honour him as a giver to the city. A monument tells you as much about the people who raised it as about the person on top. What did Bristol in 1895 choose to remember, and to forget?

explain.say: Memory is argued around the world. Look at the map. In 2015 students at the University of Cape Town won the removal of a statue of the imperialist Cecil Rhodes. Berlin built a large memorial to the murdered Jews of Europe in 2005. Hiroshima's Peace Memorial keeps the bombed dome as a warning. Why do some places add memorials while others remove them?

The French historian Pierre Nora called such places lieux de mémoire, sites of memory, where a society shapes its picture of itself. See the two sides of the statue debate. Which arguments do you find strongest, and is there a middle way?

explain.say: Bristol chose a middle way: in 2021 the statue went on show in the M Shed museum, lying down with its graffiti, beside the story of the enslaved. Thoughtful work today. Your challenge: find one monument near you, and research who raised it, when and why.

faq.a: Public history is history made for and with the public outside universities: museums, heritage sites, monuments, archives, documentaries and community projects.

faq.q: Why was the Colston statue pulled down?
faq.a: Edward Colston profited from the Royal African Company, which enslaved and transported many thousands of Africans. After years of failed campaigns to change the statue, protesters toppled it on 7 June 2020 during Black Lives Matter demonstrations.

A student protest movement that began in 2015 at the University of Cape Town, demanding removal of Cecil Rhodes's statue and wider change. The statue was removed on 9 April 2015; the movement spread to Oxford.
asks: Why did students want Rhodes's statue removed?

faq.q: Where is the Colston statue now?
faq.a: It was recovered from the harbour and, from 2021, shown at the M Shed museum in Bristol, lying down with its graffiti, alongside information about the slave trade and the protest.
asks: What happened to the Colston statue?

faq.a: Pierre Nora's term, lieux de mémoire, for places, objects, rituals and symbols through which a society remembers and shapes its identity, such as monuments, anthems or archives.
asks: What did Pierre Nora mean by lieux de memoire?

facts: Edward Colston's statue in Bristol was erected in 1895 and toppled on 7 June 2020.
The statue of Cecil Rhodes at the University of Cape Town was removed on 9 April 2015.
Berlin's Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe opened in 2005.

quiz.say: When was the Colston statue raised in Bristol?
quiz.why: It was put up in 1895, about 174 years after Colston died in 1721.

wrong.1: Colston was still alive in 1700; the statue came much later.
wrong.2: It had stood for over 50 years by 1950.

quiz.say: What does Pierre Nora's term lieux de mémoire mean?
quiz.why: Nora used it for places and symbols where a society keeps and shapes its memory.

wrong.1: Nora's term is about remembering, not lost documents.
wrong.2: Battlefields can be sites of memory, but the term is much wider.
